newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso fears seen ebbing-bankers.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso fears seen ebbing-bankers.

text.p: The Philippine peso's losses are likely to have reached a limit after last week's de facto devaluation and a mild recovery is expected, bankers said on Friday.
"There is no more of that psychological fear that it will go over 30," one foreign bank treasurer said.

The peso was rattled last Friday when the Philippine central bank announced the currency would be allowed to move in a wider range in a bid to stop weeks of speculation. The peso was seen as overvalued and speculators sold it amid attacks on other Southeast Asian currencies.
The local unit shed almost 12 percent after the decision, heading towards its weakest levels on record of more than 30.00 to the dollar.
However, on Friday morning it had recovered to 27.80 against the dollar, compared to 26.40 just ahead of the de facto devaluation.

"The freely floating peso was an answer to the doubting Thomases. This is a self-correcting market mechanism so that even the speculators find it difficult to speculate," said Omar Cruz, vice president of Citibank.
One dealer predicted a new peso trading range of 28.00/29.50 to the dollar, while another saw the peso averaging 27.50/28.00 for the rest of the year.
Confident that currency stability has returned, the central bank sliced interest rates twice in the past two days.
The central bank's key overnight borrowing rate now stands at 25 percent. The rate was boosted to a 2-1/2 year high of 32 percent in June to shield the peso from speculators.
Traders expect the overnight borrowing rate to eventually settle at around 15 percent.

The central bank has been supported by swift help from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which has offered a $1.05 billion package in the first test of its new emergency finance rules since Mexico's economic crisis 2-1/2 years ago.
"The IMF money will come in handy because it will build up the central bank's reserves," one banker said.
"The peso has to be volatile. The price of the currency has to reflect its basic supply and demand," said Jose Mario Cuyegkeng, research director of ING Barings Securities.
"The downside is that it's more difficult to do planning. But if you have a stable currency for too long, speculators build a case," Cuyegkeng said.
He noted that the central bank's previous tight grip on the peso had drained billions of dollars from reserves and caused interest rates to shoot up.
Citibank's Cruz said the peso would settle down and reflect the economy's underlying strength.
"Was there a change in fundamentals overnight? They have always been the same," he said, citing the country's low inflation, budget surplus and strong exports.
"We have seen some inflows getting into fixed income as offshore investors have already calmed down," a bank treasurer said.
Bank officials also expect the central bank to clamp down further on speculation by regulating involvement by locals in non-deliverable forwards (NDFs), which mostly operate out of Singapore.
Some bank treasurers have placed the amount of outstanding NDF peso/dollar contracts at up to $5 billion.
"The avenues for outside speculation will really be curtailed," one banker said.
